report.summary: Chunk 2 defines analyze_chunk; claims about batching and order restoration are uncheckable; ts_on is unpacked but unused in comprehension.
risks: line 127-128 | high | ts_on is unpacked but not used in the list comprehension; it is passed to analyze_file but the call includes ts_on as the last argument. If analyze_file does not expect ts_on, this will cause a TypeError. | Check analyze_file signature to confirm it accepts ts_on.

handoff.purpose: Defines analyze_chunk worker entry point for batched file analysis with index tagging.

symbols.name: analyze_chunk
symbols.note: Worker entry point; takes a tuple (ts_on, items) and returns list of (index, FileAnalysis) tuples.

claims.text: Worker entry point: analyze a batch of files, tagging each with its ORIGINAL index.
claims.why: The function returns [(i, analyze_file(...)) for i, ...] which tags each result with its original index i.

claims.text: Batched rather than one-task-per-file because Windows spawns (not forks) workers, so per-task overhead is real.
claims.why: The chunk does not contain any code related to Windows spawn vs fork or overhead analysis; this is a design justification not verifiable from the code.

claims.text: The index tag is what lets the parent restore exact input order regardless of completion order -- ``all_units`` order is load-bearing for the clone passes.
claims.why: The chunk does not contain code for the parent restoring order or any reference to all_units or clone passes; these are external to this chunk.

observations.what: The function analyze_chunk uses a tuple assignment ts_on, items = job, but ts_on is not used in the list comprehension; it is passed to analyze_file but analyze_file's signature in this chunk expects (rel, text, spec, ts_on) as per the call.
The function returns a list of tuples (int, FileAnalysis) but FileAnalysis is not defined in this chunk; its structure is unknown.
